references.text: The definition of the Passover meal as 'the Lord's Passover' (פֶּסַח) is first explained here, and verse 27 repeats this in response to the children.
The Lord explains that He will 'pass over' (פָּסַח) the houses with blood, which is the same verb used in verse 27 to explain the meaning of Passover.
The Lord passes by the door and prevents the destroyer from striking the Israelites' homes, which explains the deliverance mentioned in verse 27.
The preceding verse contains the children's question that verse 27 answers.
The actual fulfillment of the plague against Egypt's firstborn, while the Israelites were spared, as referred to in verse 27.
The people bowed down and worshiped (וַיִּקֹּד ... וַיִּשְׁתַּחֲוּ) in the same way as a response to God's deliverance.
A similar instruction to explain the meaning of Passover to future generations.
Parallel text about answering children's questions regarding God's commands and deliverance from Egypt.
A similar pattern where stones are to serve as a memorial, and parents are to explain the meaning to their children.
The psalm recounts how God struck down Egypt's firstborn, which is the event that Passover commemorates.
The Lord will 'pass over' (פָּסֹחַ) and deliver Jerusalem, using the same verb as in the Passover account.
Hebrews refers to Passover and the application of blood in faith, so that the destroyer did not touch the Israelites' firstborn.
Christ is called our Passover lamb (τὸ πάσχα ἡμῶν) who has been sacrificed, a typological fulfillment of the Passover lamb.
A clear theological contrast: The Passover sacrifice confirms the Lord's deliverance, while Ahab's offering shows misplaced trust in enemy gods.
Prophetic parallel: The historical judgment in Exodus anticipates Isaiah's prophecy that similar actions will lead Egypt to repentance.
Prophetic fulfillment: The logic of the Passover offering (salvation through sacrifice) is extended in Isaiah to also apply to Egypt.
Theological parallel: Sacrifice as a response to and means of stopping God's judgment/plague.
